factStatement: The CPU executes program instructions; it does not store programs or files permanently.
familyName: CPU role identification
measurementObjective: Given a described job inside a computer, decide whether it is the CPU that does it.
distractorStrategy: The two commonest first-year conflations: that the CPU is where files live (CPU/storage), and that the CPU is a program rather than hardware (CPU/OS). Also offer "makes the screen display images" for students who equate the CPU with everything the machine does.
notes: The anchor fact for the whole concept. Keep the phrasing plain: this is the one item a student with no background should still be able to attempt.

factStatement: The ALU carries out arithmetic and logical (comparison) operations.
familyName: Routing an operation to the unit that performs it
measurementObjective: Given a concrete operation — adding two numbers, comparing two values — name the unit that performs it.
distractorStrategy: Route the operation to the control unit (the student who thinks "control" means "does the work"), to RAM (confusing where a value is held with where it is operated on), and to the OS (confusing software instruction with hardware execution). Comparison operations are the most productive stem: many students believe only arithmetic reaches the ALU.
notes: Comparison-as-logic is the part most often missed; at least one variant should use a comparison rather than a sum.

factStatement: The control unit decodes each instruction and directs the other components; it does not compute results itself.
familyName: Separating direction from computation
measurementObjective: Distinguish the component that decides what happens next from the component that produces the value.
distractorStrategy: Attribute calculation to the control unit; attribute decoding to the ALU; claim the control unit holds the program. All three follow from reading the names rather than the behaviour.
notes: Pairs with CA_FAM02 — do not serve both in one paper. Same reassessment group for that reason.

factStatement: Registers hold the few values the CPU is working on at this instant; they are the smallest and fastest storage in the machine.
familyName: Placing registers in the storage picture
measurementObjective: Identify what registers hold and how they differ in size and speed from RAM.
distractorStrategy: Registers as "a fast part of RAM"; registers as surviving power loss; registers as larger than cache. Each is a coherent guess from someone who has only heard the word.

factStatement: RAM holds the programs and data currently in use and loses its contents when power is removed.
familyName: What RAM is for
measurementObjective: Decide what is kept in RAM and what happens to it when the machine is switched off.
distractorStrategy: "RAM keeps files permanently" — the single most common first-year error, and the one that makes the whole hierarchy incoherent. Also "RAM is where the operating system is installed" and "adding RAM makes the processor faster", both of which sound reasonable and are widely repeated.
notes: Volatility is the load-bearing half of this fact. A variant that only asks "what is RAM for" without touching persistence measures less.

factStatement: Secondary storage (disk, SSD) keeps data without power and is slower than RAM.
familyName: Choosing memory or storage for a stated need
measurementObjective: Given a requirement — survive a restart, be read as fast as possible — choose the appropriate place to keep the data.
distractorStrategy: Choose storage where speed was the requirement, and RAM where persistence was; also offer "the CPU runs the program directly from disk", which is the belief that removes the reason RAM exists.
notes: The requirement must genuinely decide the answer. A scenario whose details do not change the choice is a wording variant, not a measurement.

factStatement: From registers to cache to RAM to disk, capacity increases and speed decreases.
familyName: Ordering the hierarchy by speed and capacity
measurementObjective: Order or compare storage layers on both axes, and recognise that the two run in opposite directions.
distractorStrategy: Invert one axis while keeping the other (fastest also biggest) — the error that shows the trade-off has not landed. Also place cache above RAM in capacity, and treat the ordering as being about cost only.
notes: Spans to D4 because comparing two layers on two axes at once is genuinely multi-step, not because the words can be made longer.

conceptName: Getting data in, out and across
factStatement: Input devices bring data into the machine, output devices send it out, and some devices do both.
familyName: Classifying a device by direction of data flow
measurementObjective: Classify named devices as input, output, or both, from what the data does rather than from the device category.
distractorStrategy: Force the both-directions cases: a touchscreen classified as output only (because it is a screen), a printer that scans classified as output only, storage classified as neither. The single-direction cases are too easy to carry the item alone.
notes: A dual-direction device should appear in every variant, or the family collapses to naming.

conceptName: Getting data in, out and across
factStatement: Buses carry data, addresses and control signals between components; components do not each wire directly to every other.
familyName: How components reach each other
measurementObjective: Explain what travels between the CPU and memory, and by what shared route.
distractorStrategy: A bus that stores data rather than carrying it; components connected point to point; only data travelling, with addresses and control signals forgotten. The last is the most instructive — it is the half-formed model.

factStatement: Each instruction is fetched, then decoded, then executed, and the cycle repeats for the next instruction.
familyName: Ordering the stages of the instruction cycle
measurementObjective: Put the stages in order, or identify which stage a described action belongs to.
distractorStrategy: Decode before fetch (the student who thinks the CPU must understand an instruction before collecting it), execute before decode, and one cycle covering the whole program rather than a single instruction. The last exposes whether the repetition is understood.
notes: Order-only variants sit at D2; identifying the stage from a described action sits at D3.

factStatement: During execution, values move from memory into registers, through the ALU, and back into registers before any result returns to memory.
familyName: Tracing a value through one instruction
measurementObjective: Follow a single value through the components involved in executing one instruction, and say where it is at a given point.
distractorStrategy: The ALU reading straight from disk; a result written directly to secondary storage; the value never entering a register at all. Each removes one step, which is exactly the gap being probed.
notes: Depends on CA_F04 and CA_F10. Do not schedule this before registers and the cycle have been measured.

factStatement: All data — text, images, sound — is stored as binary; what the bits mean depends on how they are interpreted.
familyName: Reasoning about binary representation
measurementObjective: Recognise that different data types share one underlying representation, and that interpretation supplies the meaning.
distractorStrategy: Text stored as letters and images stored as pictures — the belief that storage mirrors appearance. Also "binary is only used for numbers", and "the same bits always mean the same thing", which misses interpretation.
notes: Conceptual only at Foundation. Base conversion is arithmetic and belongs with the aptitude skills, not here.

factStatement: The slowest resource on a path limits overall performance, so improving anything else changes nothing.
familyName: Diagnosing which resource is the limit
measurementObjective: Given symptoms — heavy disk activity, idle processor — identify the limiting resource and the change that would help.
distractorStrategy: Blame the CPU whatever the symptoms (the default assumption), add RAM to a disk-bound task, upgrade a component the described work never touches. All three are the reasoning error, not carelessness.
notes: The symptoms must determine the answer. Any variant where a different limiting resource would give the same answer is not measuring diagnosis.

factStatement: Hardware choices trade speed against capacity and cost; there is no option that is best on every axis.
familyName: Choosing under a stated constraint
measurementObjective: Pick the defensible configuration for a stated priority, and say what it gives up.
distractorStrategy: The fastest option regardless of the stated budget or capacity need; an option that ignores the constraint entirely; an option that claims to win on all three axes. The last tests whether the trade-off is believed at all.
notes: The constraint must be explicit and must change the answer, otherwise this degrades into "pick the biggest number".

factStatement: From registers to cache to RAM to disk, capacity increases and speed decreases.
familyName: Applying the hierarchy to an unfamiliar workload
measurementObjective: Given a workload described in terms nobody has taught — a dataset that will not fit, a value re-read constantly — decide which layer of the hierarchy the work actually depends on.
distractorStrategy: A layer that is faster but too small for the described data; one large enough but not on the path being described; the answer that would be right if the workload were reversed. The workload must decide the layer, or this collapses into CA_FAM07.
notes: Same fact as CA_FAM07, genuinely different measurement: that one orders and compares known layers, this one applies the trade-off to a situation the student has not met. Shares its reassessment group precisely because the two must never both be served.

factStatement: Every computing task takes input, processes it, and produces output.
familyName: Labelling the parts of a described task
measurementObjective: Given a described task, identify which part is the input, the processing and the output.
distractorStrategy: Swap input and output; label the processing step as input (the student who calls the whole activity "input"); offer a part of the task that is neither. Use tasks where the output is not visible on a screen, since students otherwise equate output with display.
notes: The opening fact of the skill. Everything in HCW_C02 and HCW_C03 assumes it.

factStatement: Hardware is the physical machine; software is the instructions it carries out.
familyName: Classifying a named thing as hardware or software
measurementObjective: Classify items — an operating system, a hard disk, a browser, a printer driver — on the physical/instruction distinction.
distractorStrategy: The genuinely confusing cases are the whole point: a driver (software that operates hardware), firmware, and the operating system itself, which many students place with hardware because it "comes with the machine". Obvious cases like a keyboard measure nothing.
notes: Every variant must include at least one boundary case.

factStatement: A program is a stored set of instructions; the computer does nothing the instructions do not say.
familyName: What a program is and is not
measurementObjective: Recognise that a program is instructions rather than an intelligent agent, and that unstated behaviour does not happen.
distractorStrategy: The computer "works out what was meant"; the program adapts to a case nobody wrote; a program described as data rather than instructions. The first is the misconception that survives longest and causes the most debugging confusion later.
notes: Sets up the debugging mindset that PROBLEM_SOLVING and PSEUDOCODE_FLOWCHARTS both rely on.

conceptName: A program and a running program
factStatement: A program is a file on storage; running it creates a process that occupies working memory.
familyName: Separating the stored program from the running one
measurementObjective: Say what exists before a program is launched, what exists while it runs, and what remains after it closes.
distractorStrategy: The program is deleted when closed; running twice creates one thing; the process persists after exit. All three follow from having no separation between the file and the execution.
notes: Overlaps OS_F03 by design — that one measures it from the OS side. They share no reassessment group only because the framing genuinely differs; review together before publishing.

conceptName: A program and a running program
factStatement: Working memory holds what a running program needs now; closing the program releases it.
familyName: What happens in memory as programs start and stop
measurementObjective: Predict the effect on available memory of opening and closing programs.
distractorStrategy: Memory is consumed permanently; closing a program frees disk rather than memory; memory use is fixed per machine regardless of what runs.

factStatement: Computers represent all information digitally, as numbers, whatever it looks like to a person.
familyName: Recognising digital representation
measurementObjective: Identify that text, images and sound are all held as numbers rather than as their appearance.
distractorStrategy: Each type stored "in its own way" as its appearance; only numbers being digital; images stored as physical pictures.
notes: Deliberately lighter than CA_F12 — this is recognition, that one asks about interpretation. Keep them in different papers.

factStatement: A file is data kept on storage under a name, and it survives the program that made it and the machine being switched off.
familyName: Reasoning about what survives a restart
measurementObjective: Decide which of several described pieces of data still exists after the machine is switched off and on.
distractorStrategy: Unsaved work surviving; a saved file lost on restart; open documents treated the same as saved ones. The unsaved-work case is worth using often — it is the misconception with real consequences.

factStatement: The operating system sits between applications and hardware; applications ask it for what they need rather than driving hardware themselves.
familyName: Where the OS sits between an app and the hardware
measurementObjective: Trace a described request — saving a file, printing — through application, operating system and hardware in the right order.
distractorStrategy: The application writing to the disk itself; the hardware calling the application; the OS omitted from the path entirely. Omission is the most common and the most revealing.
notes: Deliberately distinct from OS_FAM01, which measures OS responsibilities rather than position in the stack.

factStatement: An application does a particular job for a person; the operating system runs the machine for every application.
familyName: Deciding whether a job belongs to an app or the OS
measurementObjective: Given a described responsibility, decide whether an application or the operating system owns it.
distractorStrategy: Assign memory allocation or device access to an application; assign document editing to the OS; treat a bundled utility as part of the kernel because it ships with the system.

factStatement: Powering on runs firmware checks, then loads the operating system, and only then can applications start.
familyName: Ordering what happens at startup
measurementObjective: Put the startup stages in order and identify what cannot yet have happened at a given point.
distractorStrategy: Applications starting before the OS; the OS running before any hardware check; the desktop appearing first with the OS loading afterwards. The last matches what a user sees, which is why it is believed.
notes: High level only. Bootloader specifics are out of scope at Foundation.

factStatement: A network is machines connected so they can exchange data; the internet is a very large network of networks.
familyName: Distinguishing a network, the internet and the web
measurementObjective: Separate the three, and identify which is a service running on which.
distractorStrategy: The internet and the web as the same thing — near universal, and worth measuring directly. Also the browser as the internet, and email as part of the web.
notes: Overlaps COMPUTER_NETWORKS, which goes deeper. Here it is only the distinction.

factStatement: A client asks for something and a server answers; a single machine can be either, depending on the exchange.
familyName: Assigning client and server roles in an exchange
measurementObjective: In a described interaction, say which side is the client and which the server, and why.
distractorStrategy: The server as always the bigger or more distant machine; the roles as fixed properties of hardware; the client as whoever owns the data. Use a case where one machine is both, which the fixed-property model cannot handle.

factStatement: Each layer hides the detail of the layer below, which is why a program can save a file without knowing what kind of disk it is.
familyName: Recognising what a layer hides
measurementObjective: Identify what detail is deliberately hidden in a described interaction, and what would change if it were not.
distractorStrategy: Abstraction as simplification for beginners rather than as a working mechanism; the claim that lower detail is inaccessible rather than hidden; the claim that hiding detail loses capability.
notes: The most demanding fact in the skill. Expect low scores initially; that is information, not a fault.

factStatement: A stated belief about how a computer works can be judged against the input-process-output and hardware/software/OS model.
familyName: Finding the wrong step in someone's explanation
measurementObjective: Read a short explanation of how something works and identify the one step that is wrong.
distractorStrategy: Options must point at steps that ARE correct, so the student has to locate the error rather than spot an absurdity. Exactly one step is wrong, and it is wrong for a reason a student would recognise.
notes: This family does the most work in the whole skill and is the hardest to author. Every option must be defensible except one.

factStatement: An application does a particular job for a person; the operating system runs the machine for every application.
familyName: Deciding which layer should own an unfamiliar responsibility
measurementObjective: Given a capability nobody has been taught to place — scheduling a backup, limiting a download — decide whether it belongs to an application or the operating system, from the purpose of the layer rather than from memory.
distractorStrategy: The layer that could technically do it rather than the one whose purpose covers it; a placement that would make every application reimplement the same thing; a placement that would let one application affect another. Reasoning, not recall, must decide it.
notes: Same fact as HCW_FAM09, one level up: that one classifies familiar responsibilities, this one places an unfamiliar one from first principles.

factStatement: The operating system sits between applications and hardware; applications ask it for what they need rather than driving hardware themselves.
familyName: Tracing an unfamiliar request through the stack
measurementObjective: Trace a request the student has not been shown — a camera capture, a network send — through application, operating system, driver and hardware.
distractorStrategy: A path that skips the operating system; one that reverses two adjacent layers; one that inserts a layer the request never touches. Every option must be a coherent path, so the student reasons about which is real rather than eliminating nonsense.
notes: Same fact as HCW_FAM08 applied to an untaught device, which is what makes it transfer rather than recall.

conceptName: What an operating system is for
factStatement: The operating system manages the machine's resources — processor time, memory, storage, devices — on behalf of every program.
familyName: Identifying an OS responsibility
measurementObjective: Given a described job, decide whether the operating system is responsible for it.
distractorStrategy: Jobs owned by an application (spell-checking, editing an image), by hardware (performing arithmetic), or by the user. The application cases are the productive ones — students attribute anything system-looking to the OS.

conceptName: What an operating system is for
factStatement: When two programs want the same resource, the operating system decides who gets it and when.
familyName: Reasoning about contended resources
measurementObjective: Predict what happens when two programs need the same resource at once.
distractorStrategy: Both programs proceeding simultaneously with no cost; the second program failing outright; the programs negotiating between themselves. Each is a plausible model for someone who has not met arbitration.

factStatement: A process is a program in execution, with its own memory; the same program can run as several independent processes.
familyName: Comparing a program with its processes
measurementObjective: Say how many processes exist in a described situation and what each has of its own.
distractorStrategy: One program meaning one process however many windows are open; processes sharing all memory; a second copy being refused. Opening the same editor twice is the clearest stem.
notes: Related to HCW_F04 but measured differently — that asks what exists, this asks how many and with what of their own.

factStatement: On a single core the OS interleaves processes quickly rather than running them at the same instant.
familyName: How several programs appear to run at once
measurementObjective: Explain how multitasking appears simultaneous, and what limits it.
distractorStrategy: True simultaneity on one core; each program getting its own processor; the OS pausing everything else until a program finishes. The first is the belief that makes scheduling meaningless.

factStatement: The scheduler decides which ready process runs next and for how long.
familyName: Predicting what runs next
measurementObjective: Given several processes in described states, decide which can run next and why the others cannot.
distractorStrategy: Choosing a process that is waiting on input (ready and waiting conflated); strict first-come order regardless of state; the program in the front window. Include a blocked process in every variant.
notes: Named algorithms are out of scope. The measurement is readiness reasoning, not round-robin arithmetic.

factStatement: The OS gives each process memory, keeps processes out of each other's memory, and reclaims it when they end.
familyName: Reasoning about memory given to a process
measurementObjective: Decide what a process can and cannot reach in memory, and what becomes of that memory when it exits.
distractorStrategy: One process reading another's memory freely; memory never reclaimed; each process seeing all physical memory. The first is worth measuring because it is what students assume before isolation is taught.

factStatement: The filesystem organises storage into named files and directories, and the OS translates a path into a location on the device.
familyName: Reasoning about paths and locations
measurementObjective: Work out what a described path refers to, or which of several paths reaches a given file.
distractorStrategy: Absolute and relative confused; two files with the same name in different directories treated as one; the belief that moving a file changes its contents. Include one same-name pair in different directories.

factStatement: Permissions decide which users may read, change or run a file, and the OS refuses actions they do not allow.
familyName: Diagnosing a refused action
measurementObjective: Given a permission setting and an attempted action, say whether it succeeds and which permission decided it.
distractorStrategy: Read confused with execute; a permission on the file confused with one on its directory; ownership assumed to override everything. The directory case is the one that catches real confusion.
notes: Conceptual. Numeric modes are a tooling detail and do not belong at Foundation.

factStatement: The OS talks to a device through its driver, so applications need not know the make or model.
familyName: Tracing an application's use of a device
measurementObjective: Order the parts involved when an application uses a device, and identify which part knows the device specifics.
distractorStrategy: The application addressing the hardware directly; the driver as part of the application; the device needing no software at all. Ties back to HCW_F13 on abstraction.

factStatement: Ordinary programs run with limited privilege and must ask the kernel for anything that touches the machine directly.
familyName: Deciding what needs kernel privilege
measurementObjective: Given an action, decide whether a normal program may do it itself or must ask the kernel.
distractorStrategy: Any program being able to access hardware; privilege as a matter of the logged-in user only; the belief that an administrator account removes the boundary. The last conflates user rights with the privilege boundary.
notes: Grouped with permissions for reassessment: both measure "who is allowed", and serving them together would double-count.

factStatement: The OS must be running before any application can start, because applications depend on it for everything.
familyName: Reasoning about startup dependencies
measurementObjective: Identify what must already be running before a described thing can start.
distractorStrategy: An application starting first; the OS loading on demand when needed; a driver loading after the application that uses it.
notes: Distinct from HCW_FAM10, which orders the whole boot. This one is dependency reasoning.

factStatement: Running out of memory, disk or processor time produces different symptoms and needs different remedies.
familyName: Diagnosing which resource has run out
measurementObjective: Read described symptoms and identify which resource is exhausted and what would relieve it.
distractorStrategy: Attribute every slowdown to memory; free disk space to fix a memory problem; close programs to fix a full disk. Symptoms must distinguish the resources, or the item is unanswerable by reasoning.
notes: Overlaps CA_FAM13, which diagnoses a hardware bottleneck. Same shape, different subject; review together and consider one shared reassessment group.

factStatement: A command line and a graphical interface are two ways of asking the same operating system to do the same things.
familyName: Recognising interfaces as equivalent routes
measurementObjective: Decide whether a described task can be done from either interface, and what actually differs between them.
distractorStrategy: The command line as more powerful in kind rather than in convenience; the GUI as a different operating system; certain operations as impossible graphically by nature. Avoid making this a preference question.

conceptName: What an operating system is for
factStatement: The operating system manages the machine resources — processor time, memory, storage, devices — on behalf of every program.
familyName: Recognising what is and is not an operating system
measurementObjective: From named software, identify which items are operating systems.
distractorStrategy: A browser, an office suite and a file manager — the last being the productive one, because it ships with the system and looks like part of it. Avoid obscure systems: this measures the category, not brand knowledge.
notes: Added because the skill had a single recognition-level family and the plan requires ten D1 questions. Same fact as OS_FAM01: that one asks what the OS DOES, this one what one IS.

factStatement: A process is a program in execution, with its own memory; the same program can run as several independent processes.
familyName: Matching the terms program, process and application
measurementObjective: Given a definition or a described situation, choose the term that names it.
distractorStrategy: The terms used interchangeably — process for the file on disk, program for the running copy. The vocabulary itself is the measurement; the reasoning version is OS_FAM03.
notes: Same fact as OS_FAM03, deliberately at recall level so the D1 entry points are not all about responsibilities.

factStatement: The filesystem organises storage into named files and directories, and the OS translates a path into a location on the device.
familyName: Distinguishing a file from a directory
measurementObjective: Decide which described items are files and which are directories, and what a directory actually contains.
distractorStrategy: A directory described as holding data rather than entries; an extension treated as proof of being a file; a shortcut treated as the thing it points to.
notes: Same fact as OS_FAM07: that one reasons about paths, this one about the two kinds of thing a path can name.

factStatement: A problem statement contains the requirement that must be satisfied, alongside detail that does not affect it.
familyName: Extracting the actual requirement
measurementObjective: Read a short computing problem and state what must be true of a correct solution.
distractorStrategy: A restatement of the scenario rather than the requirement; a requirement the statement never made; a solution method offered in place of the requirement. The last is the commonest — students jump to how before what.
notes: Statements must be computing problems, not riddles. Irrelevant detail is legitimate here — noticing it is the skill — but it must not be arbitrary numbers with no bearing on anything.

factStatement: The inputs are the values a solution is given, distinct from values it computes for itself.
familyName: Identifying what the solution is given
measurementObjective: Separate the given inputs from intermediate and derived values.
distractorStrategy: Offer a derived value as an input (a total that must be computed), a constant as an input, and the output as an input. The derived-value case is the real measurement.

factStatement: The output is what the solution must produce, in the form the problem asks for.
familyName: Identifying what must be produced
measurementObjective: State what a correct solution returns, including its form — a count, a list, a yes or no.
distractorStrategy: The right information in the wrong form (a list where a count was asked for); an intermediate value; more than was asked. Form confusion is worth measuring — it is a real source of wrong answers later.

factStatement: A constraint rules some solutions out; a solution that ignores it is wrong however well it works otherwise.
familyName: Reasoning about what a constraint forbids
measurementObjective: Decide which of several approaches a stated constraint eliminates.
distractorStrategy: An approach that satisfies the constraint but not the requirement; one that satisfies the requirement while breaking the constraint; one eliminated by a constraint the problem never stated.
notes: The constraint must genuinely eliminate at least one otherwise-reasonable option.

factStatement: A solution can rest on an assumption the problem never granted, and it fails when that assumption does not hold.
familyName: Finding the assumption a solution relies on
measurementObjective: Identify what a described approach quietly assumes about its input.
distractorStrategy: An assumption the problem DID state; a true fact that the solution does not rely on; a restatement of the requirement. Distinguishing a relied-upon assumption from a merely true statement is the measurement.
notes: Input ordering and non-empty input are the two most productive assumptions to probe.

factStatement: A problem can be split into smaller parts that can each be solved and then combined.
familyName: Choosing a useful decomposition
measurementObjective: Choose the breakdown whose parts are independently solvable and together cover the problem.
distractorStrategy: A breakdown missing a part (does not cover the problem); one whose parts depend circularly on each other; one that restates the problem as a single step. Coverage and independence are the two things being tested.

factStatement: An example can be checked against a requirement to see whether it is consistent with it.
familyName: Judging whether an example fits the requirement
measurementObjective: Decide which of several input-and-output pairs a stated requirement actually permits.
distractorStrategy: A pair that is right for a nearby requirement; one right in value but wrong in form; one that holds for typical input but not as stated. No absurd pairs — every option must require checking.

factStatement: One input on which a rule fails disproves the rule; any number of inputs on which it works does not prove it.
familyName: Choosing an input that breaks a claim
measurementObjective: Given a claimed rule, select the input that shows it wrong.
distractorStrategy: Inputs on which the rule holds; an input that breaks a different rule; an input the problem excludes. The asymmetry between proving and disproving is the fact being measured, so several options should be perfectly valid inputs on which the rule works.
notes: One of the highest-value families in Foundation: it underpins testing, debugging and edge cases alike.

factStatement: A rule can be inferred from worked examples and then stated so it applies beyond them.
familyName: Inferring the rule behind the examples
measurementObjective: Read several input-output pairs and state the rule that produced them.
distractorStrategy: A rule that fits some pairs but not all — the important distractor, because it is what a student who stopped checking early would choose. Also a rule that fits every pair but is more specific than the data supports.
notes: Computing-flavoured: rules over lists, strings or counts. Not number-sequence puzzles, which belong to the aptitude skills.

factStatement: Different approaches solve the same problem, and the problem's shape decides which is appropriate.
familyName: Choosing an approach that fits the problem
measurementObjective: Select the approach that satisfies the requirement given the stated shape of the input.
distractorStrategy: An approach that works only on sorted input where none is promised; one that solves a related but different problem; one correct but disallowed by a stated constraint.

factStatement: Values change as a procedure runs, and the result depends on their values at each step.
familyName: Tracing values through a described procedure
measurementObjective: Follow a short described procedure over given input and state the value held at a named point.
distractorStrategy: The value one step early or late (off-by-one in the trace); the final value where an intermediate was asked; a value from the wrong variable. Language-independent — the procedure is described, not coded.
notes: Overlaps PF_FAM04 which traces pseudocode. Keep separate: this is prose, that is notation. Same reassessment consideration.

factStatement: The inputs that break a solution are usually the empty, single, duplicate, boundary or extreme cases.
familyName: Finding the input a solution has not considered
measurementObjective: Given a described approach, identify the input most likely to break it.
distractorStrategy: Typical inputs it handles perfectly well; a large input where size is not the issue; an invalid input the problem excludes. The distractors must be inputs a careless reader would call risky.

factStatement: The difference between expected and actual behaviour points to which step is wrong.
familyName: Locating the faulty step from the symptom
measurementObjective: Given a procedure and a wrong result, identify the step responsible.
distractorStrategy: Steps that are correct as written; a step that would cause a different symptom; the input blamed rather than the procedure. Exactly one step must explain the observed symptom specifically.
notes: The symptom must discriminate. If two steps could produce it, the item has two defensible answers.

factStatement: Two correct solutions can differ in work done, and one may be preferable on a stated ground.
familyName: Comparing two correct solutions
measurementObjective: Given two working approaches and a stated priority, choose the better and say why.
distractorStrategy: A preference on a ground the question did not state; an incorrect solution offered as more efficient; a claim that they are equivalent when the priority distinguishes them. Both options must genuinely work.
notes: Efficiency AWARENESS only — more or less work, not complexity notation, which is not taught at Foundation.

factStatement: A useful test can distinguish a correct solution from an incorrect one; a test both pass tells you nothing.
familyName: Choosing a test that would catch the fault
measurementObjective: Select the input whose result would reveal whether a described solution is wrong.
distractorStrategy: Tests that pass under both the correct and the faulty version — the key distractor, since choosing one shows testing is understood as "running it" rather than as discrimination. Also a test outside the stated input domain.
notes: Pairs closely with PS_FAM08 on counterexamples; the two share the discrimination idea and should not appear together.

factStatement: A problem statement contains the requirement that must be satisfied, alongside detail that does not affect it.
familyName: Telling a requirement from a method
measurementObjective: Given several statements about a task, identify the one that says WHAT must be true rather than HOW to achieve it.
distractorStrategy: A method stated as though it were the goal (go through the list one by one); a constraint offered as the requirement; a restatement of the input. Students conflate goal and method constantly, and this is the cheapest place to detect it.
notes: Same fact as PS_FAM01 at recognition level. Added because the only two families reaching D1 were both about inputs and outputs.

factStatement: A constraint rules some solutions out; a solution that ignores it is wrong however well it works otherwise.
familyName: Spotting the constraint in a statement
measurementObjective: Identify which part of a problem statement is a constraint rather than a requirement or incidental context.
distractorStrategy: The requirement offered as a constraint; context with no bearing on any solution; an implementation preference. Recognition first, then PS_FAM04 measures reasoning about what it forbids.
notes: Same fact as PS_FAM04, recognition rather than elimination.

factStatement: Each flowchart shape means one kind of step: terminator, process, decision, input/output.
familyName: Matching a step to its symbol
measurementObjective: Given a described step, name the symbol that represents it, or the reverse.
distractorStrategy: Process and input/output swapped (both are "doing something" to a beginner); decision used for any step involving a value; terminator used for any first step including an input. Reading a value is the most productive stem.
notes: The only pure-recall family in this skill. Everything else requires reading a diagram or a trace.

factStatement: Arrows show the order steps happen in, and a decision has one arrow out for each outcome.
familyName: Reading the order from the arrows
measurementObjective: Say which step follows another, including which branch is taken for a given outcome.
distractorStrategy: Reading top-to-bottom while ignoring an arrow that loops back; taking both branches of a decision; treating position on the page as order. The loop-back case separates reading from assuming.

factStatement: Assignment stores a value in a variable, replacing what was there; the order of assignments changes the result.
familyName: What a variable holds after a sequence of assignments
measurementObjective: Say what a variable holds after a short sequence, where order matters.
distractorStrategy: The first value assigned rather than the last (assignment read as declaration); both values as though the variable accumulated; the value a swap would give if a temporary had been used. The swap-without-temporary case is especially productive.

factStatement: An input step brings a value in from outside; an output step reports one; neither changes anything else.
familyName: What an input or output step does
measurementObjective: Distinguish reading a value from reporting one, and say what each leaves changed.
distractorStrategy: Output believed to change the variable; input believed to display it; both treated as processing steps.

factStatement: A condition is evaluated to true or false, and exactly one branch runs.
familyName: Deciding which branch runs for a given input
measurementObjective: For given input, say which branch executes and therefore what the result is.
distractorStrategy: Both branches running; the else branch running when the condition is true; a boundary value sent the wrong way. Every variant should include a value on the boundary, since that is where the misconception lives.

factStatement: The condition written decides which inputs take which path, so a stated rule determines the condition needed.
familyName: Choosing the condition that implements a stated rule
measurementObjective: Given a rule in words, choose the condition that implements it exactly, including its boundary.
distractorStrategy: Strict where inclusive was meant and the reverse — the single most valuable distractor in this skill; a condition with the comparison reversed; one correct for typical values but wrong at the boundary.
notes: The boundary must be the discriminator. A rule whose boundary never arises does not measure this.

factStatement: A loop repeats while its condition holds; the condition is checked each time round.
familyName: How many times a loop body runs
measurementObjective: Say how many times a loop body executes for given starting values.
distractorStrategy: One iteration too many or too few (the off-by-one, which is the point); zero when the condition is false at entry misread as one; the count of the range rather than of the executions.
notes: Include a loop whose body never runs. Students often believe a loop always executes at least once.

factStatement: A counter records how many times something happened; an accumulator builds up a running result. They are different jobs.
familyName: Telling a counter from an accumulator
measurementObjective: Identify which variable counts and which accumulates, and what each holds at the end.
distractorStrategy: The two swapped; the accumulator reported as the count; either initialised wrongly so the first iteration is lost. Averaging is the ideal stem, since it needs both.

factStatement: Following pseudocode step by step over given input produces exactly one output.
familyName: Predicting the output of a short algorithm
measurementObjective: Trace a short pseudocode fragment over stated input and give the printed result.
distractorStrategy: The result of one extra or one missing iteration; an intermediate value printed instead of the final; the answer that follows from misreading the condition. Every distractor should be reachable by one specific slip.
notes: The single most valuable family in this skill: it cannot be answered without actually tracing.

factStatement: The values of every variable at each step can be written out as a table, and the table determines the result.
familyName: Completing a trace table
measurementObjective: Give the value of a named variable after a stated iteration.
distractorStrategy: The value from the adjacent iteration; the value before rather than after the update; another variable's value at the same step. Asking about a middle iteration rather than the last is what makes this distinct from output prediction.
notes: Do not serve alongside PF_FAM09 — same reassessment group for that reason.

factStatement: The same algorithm can be written as pseudocode or drawn as a flowchart, with the same behaviour.
familyName: Matching pseudocode to the flowchart that means the same
measurementObjective: Given one form, choose the other that behaves identically.
distractorStrategy: A version with the branches swapped; one with the loop condition checked at the end rather than the start; one differing only at the boundary. Every option must be a well-formed algorithm — the difference must be behavioural.

factStatement: An algorithm with a step missing produces a predictably wrong result, and the missing step can be recovered from it.
familyName: Supplying the step that makes it correct
measurementObjective: Given an algorithm with a gap and its intended behaviour, choose the step that completes it.
distractorStrategy: A step that fixes typical input but not the boundary; one that belongs at a different position; a plausible step that leaves the counter or accumulator wrong. The gap must have exactly one correct filling.
notes: This is where a blank belongs — a gap in an algorithm, with the intended behaviour stated. It is not the "____" of a fill-in-the-sentence stem.

factStatement: An algorithm can run without failing and still be wrong, and the way it is wrong identifies the faulty step.
familyName: Finding the logic error behind a wrong result
measurementObjective: Given an algorithm and a wrong output, identify the step that caused it.
distractorStrategy: Steps that are correct; a step whose fault would give a different wrong answer; a syntax-style complaint where the error is logical. The observed output must implicate exactly one step.
notes: Classic sources: accumulator initialised inside the loop, condition off by one, update placed after the output.

factStatement: Empty, single-item and boundary inputs are where an otherwise-correct algorithm misbehaves.
familyName: Tracing an algorithm on an extreme input
measurementObjective: Say what a given algorithm does on empty, single-item or boundary input.
distractorStrategy: The answer for typical input; the answer assuming the loop runs at least once; a plausible crash where the algorithm actually returns a wrong value quietly. The quiet-wrong-answer option is the most instructive.
notes: The hardest family in the skill and the most diagnostic. Empty input on a loop with an accumulator is the canonical stem.

factStatement: A counter records how many times something happened; an accumulator builds up a running result. They are different jobs.
familyName: Recognising a variable role from how it is updated
measurementObjective: From a single update line, say whether the variable is counting or accumulating.
distractorStrategy: A counter and an accumulator whose update lines differ only in what is added — one a fixed step, the other the current value. That is the entire distinction and it is visible in one line.
notes: Same fact as PF_FAM08 at recognition level, giving the skill a third D1 family. The update line may be shown as pseudocode inside the stem.

factStatement: Assignment stores the value on the right into the name on the left; it is not a statement of equality.
familyName: Reading an assignment in the right direction
measurementObjective: Say which name changes and which value it takes, given a single assignment.
distractorStrategy: The assignment read right-to-left; both names claimed to change; the assignment read as asserting the two are now permanently equal. The last is the belief that later makes x = x + 1 look impossible.
notes: Show real code in the stem. x = y is the whole item; no scenario is needed and none should be added.

factStatement: Every value has a type, and the type is visible in how the value is written.
familyName: Naming the type of a written value
measurementObjective: Given literals as they appear in code, name each type.
distractorStrategy: The productive cases are "5" against 5, 5 against 5.0, and True against "True". A student who reads past the quotes gets all three wrong, which is exactly the confusion that breaks input handling later.
notes: Quoted digits must appear in every variant.

factStatement: An output statement displays a value and changes nothing else.
familyName: What one output statement produces
measurementObjective: Give exactly what a single output statement prints.
distractorStrategy: The variable name printed rather than its value; the value with quotes where there are none; the value the variable held before the preceding assignment.
notes: The D1 entry point for the skill. One or two lines only.

factStatement: Assignment stores the value on the right into the name on the left; it is not a statement of equality.
familyName: Tracing one variable through several assignments
measurementObjective: Give the value a named variable holds after a short run of assignments where order matters.
distractorStrategy: The first value assigned rather than the last; the value from the line before the one asked about; the result of applying the assignments in written order to the wrong variable.
notes: Same fact as PGF_FAM01, different measurement: that one is answerable from a definition, this one only by tracing. Same reassessment group so they are never served together.

factStatement: An expression is evaluated to a single value before it is stored or displayed.
familyName: Evaluating an expression to its value
measurementObjective: Give the value an expression produces, including its type.
distractorStrategy: The right number as the wrong type; the operands combined in written order ignoring precedence; the expression left unevaluated as text.

factStatement: Operator precedence decides the order of evaluation, and brackets override it.
familyName: Working out which operation happens first
measurementObjective: Evaluate an expression whose result depends on precedence, or choose the bracketing that gives a stated result.
distractorStrategy: Strict left-to-right evaluation — the answer that reveals precedence has not landed. Also the correct precedence with one operator misread, and a bracketing that changes the result in the other direction.
notes: The expression must give different answers under left-to-right and under precedence, or the item measures arithmetic instead.

factStatement: Every value has a type, and the type is visible in how the value is written.
familyName: How type changes what an operator does
measurementObjective: Predict the result of the same operator applied to different types.
distractorStrategy: "5" + "5" answered as 10 — the single most valuable distractor in this skill. Also numeric addition where concatenation happens, and an error claimed where the operation is perfectly legal.
notes: Same fact as PGF_FAM02: that one names types, this one shows why naming them matters.

factStatement: Input arrives as text and must be converted before it can be used as a number.
familyName: Reasoning about unconverted input
measurementObjective: Predict what happens when input is used without conversion, and what conversion is needed.
distractorStrategy: Arithmetic succeeding on unconverted input; concatenation of two inputs reported as a sum (the classic "2" + "3" giving "23"); a crash where the language quietly concatenates instead.
notes: This family catches the single commonest first-program bug. Worth several items.

factStatement: Statements run in order, and reordering them can change the result.
familyName: How reordering statements changes the outcome
measurementObjective: Given two orderings of the same statements, say whether the results differ and how.
distractorStrategy: Claiming the orders are equivalent when they are not; claiming they differ when the statements are genuinely independent. Include one pair that IS equivalent, or the family teaches that order always matters.

factStatement: Division, integer division and remainder are different operations and give different results.
familyName: Distinguishing the division operators
measurementObjective: Give the result of each division-family operator on the same operands.
distractorStrategy: The float answer where integer division was used and the reverse; the remainder where the quotient was asked; a rounded result where truncation happens. Negative operands are the D4 case and separate rule-following from memory.
notes: Foundation-critical rather than trivia: this is where counting and averaging code silently goes wrong.

factStatement: A program can refuse to run, stop while running, or run to completion and be wrong; these are different failures.
familyName: Classifying how a program failed
measurementObjective: Given a fragment and what happened, classify the failure and say when it was detected.
distractorStrategy: A logic error reported as a crash; a runtime failure attributed to syntax; the claim that a program producing output cannot be wrong. The last is the belief this family exists to break.

factStatement: Using a variable before anything has been stored in it fails; initialising it in the wrong place has the same effect.
familyName: Diagnosing a missing or misplaced initialisation
measurementObjective: Identify why a fragment fails or gives a wrong total, given where its variables are initialised.
distractorStrategy: Blame the arithmetic rather than the initialisation; blame the input; propose an initialisation in a position that would still be wrong. The accumulator initialised inside a loop is the canonical stem.

factStatement: Copying one variable into another does not link them; changing one afterwards leaves the other alone.
familyName: Tracing several interacting variables
measurementObjective: Give the values of all named variables after a fragment where one is copied and then changed.
distractorStrategy: Both variables updated as though linked; the swap performed without the temporary so one value is lost; the values from one step earlier. A three-variable rotation is the D5 case.
notes: Swap-without-temporary is the highest-value stem here and belongs in most variants.

factStatement: Zero, negative, empty and boundary inputs are where a fragment that works on ordinary values stops working.
familyName: Predicting behaviour on an extreme input
measurementObjective: Say what a fragment does on zero, negative or empty input.
distractorStrategy: The answer for ordinary input; a crash where the code quietly returns something wrong; a wrong value where it genuinely does crash. Distinguishing a quiet wrong answer from a failure is the measurement.
notes: Division by a computed zero is the canonical D5 stem: the zero must be arrived at, not written.

factStatement: Two fragments written differently can behave identically, and two written similarly can not.
familyName: Judging whether two fragments behave the same
measurementObjective: Decide whether two fragments produce the same result for every input, and name the input that separates them if not.
distractorStrategy: A pair differing only at a boundary; a pair differing only on empty input; a pair that genuinely is equivalent despite looking different. Every option must be plausible on typical input.
notes: The separating input must exist and be findable. If no input distinguishes them, the answer is "equivalent" and the item still works.

factStatement: Python literals carry their type in how they are written: 5, 5.0, "5" and True are four different values.
familyName: Naming a Python literal type
measurementObjective: Name the type of each of several Python literals shown in code.
distractorStrategy: "5" called an int, 5.0 called an int, True called a string. All three come from reading the value and ignoring how it is written.

factStatement: print displays the value of what it is given, without the quotes of a string literal.
familyName: What a single print produces
measurementObjective: Give exactly what one or two print statements output.
distractorStrategy: Output shown with quotes; the variable name printed instead of its value; two prints shown on one line when they produce two.
notes: Whether the output occupies one line or two is a real distinction and worth measuring.

factStatement: A Python name may contain letters, digits and underscores but may not begin with a digit, and case matters.
familyName: Deciding whether a name is usable
measurementObjective: Identify which of several names Python accepts.
distractorStrategy: A name beginning with a digit; one containing a hyphen; two names differing only in case treated as the same. The case pair is the one that matters, because it causes real bugs rather than a refusal to run.
notes: Admitted as Foundation-critical rather than trivia: a beginner blocked by an invalid name cannot proceed at all.

factStatement: Assigning to a name again replaces what it referred to, whatever the type of either value.
familyName: Tracing Python assignments
measurementObjective: Give what a name refers to after a short sequence of assignments, including one that changes type.
distractorStrategy: The earlier value; an error claimed for the type change (Python permits it, and believing otherwise is a real misconception); the two values combined.

factStatement: String positions start at zero, and a negative index counts from the end.
familyName: Indexing into a string
measurementObjective: Give the character or slice a given index or slice expression produces.
distractorStrategy: One-based indexing; the slice end treated as inclusive; a negative index counted from the wrong end. Off-by-one is the whole family.

factStatement: String methods return a new string and leave the original unchanged.
familyName: What a string method returns and what it leaves
measurementObjective: Give the result of a string method call, and say what the original variable holds afterwards.
distractorStrategy: The original reported as modified in place — the misconception this family exists for. Also the wrong case for a case-changing method, and whitespace not removed where strip was called. Options must preserve case exactly: the case IS the answer.
notes: A case-sensitivity item cannot have its options compared case-insensitively anywhere in the pipeline.

factStatement: A list can be changed in place, and two names can refer to the same list.
familyName: Reasoning about a changed list
measurementObjective: Give the contents of each named list after an in-place change, where two names may refer to one list.
distractorStrategy: The second name treated as an independent copy — the central misconception. Also the change applied to the wrong position, and an error claimed where mutation is legal.
notes: The aliasing case is the D4 measurement and should not be diluted with plain indexing variants.

factStatement: input always returns a string, whatever the user typed.
familyName: Reasoning about the type input returns
measurementObjective: Predict the result of arithmetic or comparison on a value taken straight from input.
distractorStrategy: Numeric addition of two inputs reported as a sum rather than a concatenation; a comparison against a number reported as working; a crash where concatenation quietly succeeds.

factStatement: Converting a string to a number succeeds only if the text is a number.
familyName: What conversion does and when it fails
measurementObjective: Say what a conversion produces for given text, including when it fails.
distractorStrategy: int("3.5") reported as 3 rather than failing — the most instructive case. Also a failure claimed for text that converts fine, and a float conversion reported as truncating.

factStatement: In Python / gives a float, // truncates toward negative infinity, and % gives a remainder.
familyName: Distinguishing /, // and %
measurementObjective: Give the result and type of each division-family operator on the same operands.
distractorStrategy: 7 / 2 reported as 3; 7 // 2 reported as 3.5; the remainder confused with the quotient. Negative operands are the D4 case, since -7 // 2 is not -3.
notes: The float result of / is Python-specific and catches students transferring from C.

factStatement: Zero, the empty string and the empty list are false in a condition; other values of those types are true.
familyName: Deciding the truth value of a non-boolean
measurementObjective: Say whether a condition holds when the value tested is not a boolean.
distractorStrategy: An error claimed for testing a non-boolean; zero treated as true because it exists; the string "False" treated as false. The last is a genuine and common confusion.

factStatement: Indexing beyond the end of a sequence fails; the last valid index is one less than the length.
familyName: Diagnosing an out-of-range access
measurementObjective: Identify why an access fails and what the largest valid index was.
distractorStrategy: The length given as the last valid index; the failure blamed on the value rather than the position; a loop bound reported as safe when it reaches the length.

factStatement: A fragment combining assignment, a condition and a loop produces one determinate output.
familyName: Tracing a fragment that combines several constructs
measurementObjective: Give the printed output of a short fragment using assignment, a condition and a loop together.
distractorStrategy: The result of one extra or one fewer iteration; the value printed before the final update; the answer from taking the other branch. Each distractor must be reachable by one identifiable slip.
notes: The strongest family in the skill: it cannot be answered without tracing. D5 uses an unfamiliar combination rather than more lines.

factStatement: An empty string or list makes loops run zero times and makes some operations fail.
familyName: Behaviour on an empty sequence
measurementObjective: Say what a fragment does when its sequence is empty.
distractorStrategy: The loop assumed to run once; an initialised accumulator reported as an error; a crash where the code returns the initial value quietly. The last is the most instructive, since a silent zero is worse than a failure.
notes: Averaging an empty list is the canonical stem: it separates a quiet wrong answer from a division failure.

factStatement: Two expressions can give the same result on some inputs and differ on others.
familyName: Judging whether two expressions always agree
measurementObjective: Decide whether two expressions agree for every input, and name a value where they differ.
distractorStrategy: Pairs that agree on positive integers and differ on zero, on negatives, or between int and float. Every option must look interchangeable at a glance.

factStatement: Each comparison operator has a precise meaning, and the ones including equality differ from the ones excluding it.
familyName: Reading a comparison operator
measurementObjective: Say whether a given comparison is true for stated values, including at the boundary.
distractorStrategy: Strict and inclusive swapped at the boundary; == confused with =; a comparison reported as an error. Every variant should include equal operands, since that is where the operators separate.
notes: Equal operands must appear, or the item cannot distinguish < from <=.

factStatement: A condition evaluates to true or false, and that value can be stored like any other.
familyName: Recognising a boolean result
measurementObjective: Identify what a comparison produces and what type it is.
distractorStrategy: The comparison reported as producing one of its operands; the result as the string "True"; the claim that a comparison cannot be stored.

factStatement: Exactly one branch of an if/else runs, and code after the conditional runs either way.
familyName: Identifying which lines are inside a branch
measurementObjective: Given an indented fragment, say which lines run conditionally and which always run.
distractorStrategy: A line after the conditional treated as part of the last branch — the indentation misreading that causes real bugs. Also both branches claimed to run, and neither.
notes: Show indentation exactly. This family measures reading structure, so the structure must be visible.

factStatement: A condition is evaluated against the current values of its variables.
familyName: Evaluating a condition on given values
measurementObjective: Say whether a condition holds for stated variable values.
distractorStrategy: Evaluation against the values before an intervening assignment; the comparison reversed; a boundary sent the wrong way.

factStatement: Exactly one branch of an if/else runs, and code after the conditional runs either way.
familyName: Deciding which branch runs and what it prints
measurementObjective: Give the output of a conditional fragment for stated input.
distractorStrategy: The other branch taken; both branches printed; the code after the conditional omitted. Include boundary input in most variants.
notes: Same fact as CB_FAM03, different measurement: that one reads structure, this one runs it.

factStatement: else runs when no earlier condition held, and an if with no else may run nothing at all.
familyName: What happens when no condition holds
measurementObjective: Say what a fragment does for input that satisfies none of its conditions.
distractorStrategy: The first branch assumed to run as a default; an error claimed for an if with no else; the last branch treated as a catch-all when it has its own condition.

factStatement: In a chain, conditions are tested in order and the first true one wins, so reordering changes the result.
familyName: How the order of a chain changes the outcome
measurementObjective: Say which branch a value reaches in a chain, and what reordering would change.
distractorStrategy: A later branch reached although an earlier condition also held — the misconception that all matching branches run. Also a reordering claimed harmless when it changes the result for overlapping ranges.
notes: Overlapping ranges are essential; a chain of disjoint conditions cannot measure order.

factStatement: and requires both parts, or requires either, and not inverts.
familyName: Evaluating a combined condition
measurementObjective: Say whether a combined condition holds for stated values.
distractorStrategy: and and or swapped; not applied to the wrong part; a condition true for one part reported as true overall under and. The D4 case negates a combined condition, where students distribute not incorrectly.

factStatement: Whether a boundary value is included depends on whether the operator includes equality.
familyName: What happens exactly at the boundary
measurementObjective: Say what a fragment does for input exactly equal to its threshold.
distractorStrategy: The behaviour just below or just above the boundary; the boundary assumed included; a gap where two conditions both exclude it. The uncovered-boundary case is the most valuable.
notes: This family carries the most weight in the skill: nearly every real conditional bug is a boundary.

factStatement: An inner condition is only reached when the outer one held.
familyName: Tracing nested conditions
measurementObjective: Give the output of a nested conditional for stated input.
distractorStrategy: The inner branch reached although the outer failed; the inner else attached to the outer if; the output for the sibling case. Indentation must be exact and must matter.

factStatement: A rule stated in words determines exactly one correct condition, including at its boundary.
familyName: Choosing the condition that implements a rule
measurementObjective: Given a rule in words, choose the condition that implements it exactly.
distractorStrategy: Strict where inclusive was meant; the comparison reversed; a condition correct for typical values and wrong at the edge. "At least" and "more than" in the rule text are the discriminators.

factStatement: A conditional that gives the wrong answer for particular inputs points to a specific fault in its conditions.
familyName: Finding the fault from which inputs are wrong
measurementObjective: Given a fragment and the inputs it handles wrongly, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: Faults that would produce a different wrong set; correct parts of the condition; the input blamed rather than the condition. The set of failing inputs must implicate exactly one fault.
notes: Stating WHICH inputs are wrong is what makes this diagnosis rather than inspection.

factStatement: A branch can be impossible to reach because an earlier condition already covers every value that would satisfy it.
familyName: Spotting a branch that can never run
measurementObjective: Identify which branch of a chain is unreachable and why.
distractorStrategy: A branch that is merely rare; one reachable only at a boundary; the claim that all branches are reachable. Requires reasoning over the whole chain, not one line.

factStatement: Two differently written conditions can select exactly the same values, or differ only at an edge.
familyName: Judging whether two conditions select the same values
measurementObjective: Decide whether two conditions are equivalent, and name a value that separates them if not.
distractorStrategy: A pair differing only at the boundary; a negation distributed incorrectly over and/or; a pair that genuinely is equivalent. All options must look interchangeable.
notes: De Morgan without naming it: not (a and b) against (not a) or (not b) is the canonical D5 pair.

factStatement: A loop runs its body more than once instead of the code being written out repeatedly.
familyName: Recognising what a loop replaces
measurementObjective: Identify which repeated code a loop replaces, or which task needs one.
distractorStrategy: A task with a fixed, known number of distinct steps offered as needing a loop; a loop claimed to run its body once; a conditional offered as repetition.

conceptName: The values a loop runs over
factStatement: A range from 0 to n produces n values, ending one before n.
familyName: Listing the values a range produces
measurementObjective: Give the values a stated range yields.
distractorStrategy: The end value included; counting from one; n+1 values. Inclusion of the end is the entire measurement and every distractor should turn on it.
notes: The one fact that, misunderstood, makes every subsequent loop item wrong.

factStatement: A counted loop suits a known number of repetitions; a conditional loop suits repeating until something becomes true.
familyName: Choosing the kind of loop a task needs
measurementObjective: Given a described repetition, choose the loop form that fits.
distractorStrategy: A counted loop chosen where the count is not known in advance; a conditional loop where the count is fixed; the claim that only one form exists. Keep it about fit, not preference.

conceptName: The values a loop runs over
factStatement: A range from 0 to n produces n values, ending one before n.
familyName: How many times the body runs
measurementObjective: Give the number of times a loop body executes for stated bounds.
distractorStrategy: One too many or one too few; the difference between the bounds where a step is involved; the count of values rather than executions where a break is present.
notes: Same fact as LP_FAM02, applied rather than recalled.

factStatement: The loop variable takes a new value each time round and holds its final value after the loop.
familyName: What the loop variable holds at a given point
measurementObjective: Give the loop variable value during a named iteration and after the loop finishes.
distractorStrategy: The value one iteration out; the end bound rather than the last value taken; the initial value. The after-the-loop case is the productive one.

factStatement: An accumulator adds each value to a running result and must be initialised before the loop.
familyName: What an accumulator holds at the end
measurementObjective: Give the accumulator value after the loop, for stated input.
distractorStrategy: The result of initialising inside the loop, so only the last value survives — the single most valuable distractor. Also the count instead of the total, and the total missing the first or last item.

factStatement: A counter increases by a fixed step each time a condition is met, counting occurrences rather than summing values.
familyName: What a counter holds at the end
measurementObjective: Give the counter value after a loop that counts only matching items.
distractorStrategy: The total of the matching values rather than how many; every item counted regardless of the condition; the count off by one from initialising at one.
notes: A loop needing both a counter and an accumulator — an average — is the strongest D4 stem.

factStatement: A conditional loop stops only when something inside it makes the condition false.
familyName: Reasoning about whether a loop stops
measurementObjective: Decide whether a loop terminates for stated input and what makes it stop.
distractorStrategy: Termination claimed where nothing changes the condition; non-termination claimed where the update is inside a branch that does run; the loop assumed to stop after a fixed number of turns regardless.

factStatement: If the condition is false at entry the body never runs, and whatever it would have set keeps its initial value.
familyName: What happens when the loop does not run
measurementObjective: Give the output of a loop whose condition is false before the first iteration.
distractorStrategy: The body assumed to run once — the misconception this family exists for. Also an error claimed, and the value the loop would have produced had it run.

factStatement: An inner loop runs fully for each iteration of the outer one.
familyName: How many times a nested body runs
measurementObjective: Give the total executions of the inner body, or the output of a nested pair.
distractorStrategy: The bounds added rather than multiplied; the inner loop counted once; the count when the inner bound depends on the outer variable computed as though it were fixed.
notes: A dependent inner bound is the D4 case and much stronger than two fixed bounds.

factStatement: break leaves the loop immediately, skipping the rest of the body and all remaining iterations.
familyName: What break skips
measurementObjective: Give the output of a loop containing a break, for stated input.
distractorStrategy: break treated as skipping one iteration (confusing it with continue) — the central confusion; the rest of the body after break assumed to run; break in a nested loop assumed to leave both.
notes: Foundation-appropriate as behaviour, not as style advice.

factStatement: continue abandons the rest of this iteration and starts the next one.
familyName: What continue skips
measurementObjective: Give the output of a loop containing a continue.
distractorStrategy: continue treated as leaving the loop; the skipped statements assumed to run anyway; a counter after the continue assumed to have been reached. Pairing it with a counter placed after the continue is the strongest stem.

factStatement: A loop that never ends has a condition nothing in the body can make false.
familyName: Finding why a loop never ends
measurementObjective: Identify the line whose absence or placement causes a loop not to terminate.
distractorStrategy: Lines that are correct; an update present but inside a branch that never runs; the condition blamed when the update is the fault. The D5 case makes the update reachable but ineffective.

factStatement: A loop processing one item too many or too few has a bound or a starting value one out.
familyName: Diagnosing an off-by-one from the result
measurementObjective: Given a loop and a result one out from expected, identify what to change.
distractorStrategy: A change that fixes the count but breaks the values; one that moves the error to the other end; a change to the accumulator where the bound is at fault. Several options must plausibly shift the result by one.
notes: The commonest real loop bug, and the one most worth measuring at transfer level.

factStatement: Empty and single-item input are where a loop that works on ordinary input misbehaves.
familyName: Tracing a loop on empty or single-item input
measurementObjective: Say what a loop produces for empty or single-item input.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary-input answer; a failure where the initial value is returned quietly; a value where it genuinely fails. Finding a maximum with the accumulator initialised to zero is the canonical stem, since it returns a plausible wrong answer for all-negative input.

factStatement: A function gives a name to a piece of work so it can be used repeatedly without being rewritten.
familyName: Recognising what a function achieves
measurementObjective: Identify what defining a function gives you that repeating the code does not.
distractorStrategy: A function claimed to make code run faster; claimed to be required by the language; claimed to run on its own once defined. The last is a real belief and leads to confusion about calls.

factStatement: Defining a function does not run it; the body runs only when the function is called.
familyName: Telling a definition from a call
measurementObjective: Say whether a fragment produces output, given that it defines a function and may or may not call it.
distractorStrategy: The body assumed to run at the point of definition — the misconception this family exists for. Also the body assumed to run once per definition and once per call.
notes: A fragment that defines but never calls is the sharpest stem: the correct answer is that nothing is printed.

factStatement: A parameter is the name in the definition; an argument is the value supplied at the call.
familyName: Distinguishing a parameter from an argument
measurementObjective: Given a definition and a call, identify which names are parameters and which values are arguments.
distractorStrategy: The terms swapped; the return value called an argument; a variable outside the function called a parameter. The vocabulary matters because every later error message uses it.

factStatement: A call suspends the caller, runs the body, and resumes the caller where it left off.
familyName: Tracing the order of execution across a call
measurementObjective: Give the order in which output appears when a function is called mid-way through other code.
distractorStrategy: The function output placed first because the definition appears first; the caller output shown entirely before the callee; output ordered by line number rather than by execution.
notes: Definition placed above the call, and output interleaved, so line order and execution order genuinely differ.

factStatement: Arguments are matched to parameters by position, so their order matters.
familyName: Matching arguments to parameters
measurementObjective: Give the result of a call where swapping the arguments would change the answer.
distractorStrategy: The arguments bound in reverse; binding by name similarity rather than position; an error claimed where the call is valid. The operation must be non-commutative, or the swap is undetectable.
notes: Subtraction or division in the body; never addition.

factStatement: return sends a value back to the caller and ends the function immediately.
familyName: What the caller receives
measurementObjective: Give what a call evaluates to, and what happens to code after the return.
distractorStrategy: Code after the return assumed to run; the returned value assumed to be printed; the last computed value returned rather than the one named. A return inside a loop is the D4 case.

factStatement: A function with no return gives back nothing usable, even if it printed something.
familyName: What a function without a return gives back
measurementObjective: Say what the caller receives from a function that prints but does not return.
distractorStrategy: The printed value assumed to be returned — the single most valuable distractor in this skill. Also the last assignment inside the body assumed to be returned, and an error claimed at the point of definition.
notes: The print/return confusion is the defining Foundation error with functions.

factStatement: Each call starts fresh; values from a previous call do not carry over.
familyName: Reasoning about repeated calls
measurementObjective: Give the results of two successive calls to the same function.
distractorStrategy: The second call assumed to continue from the first, so a local counter appears to accumulate; both calls assumed to return the first result; an error claimed on the second call.

factStatement: A name created inside a function exists only while it runs and cannot be used outside.
familyName: What is visible outside a function
measurementObjective: Say whether a name is available after the function returns, and what happens if it is used.
distractorStrategy: The local assumed visible outside; the local assumed to overwrite an outer name of the same name; the value assumed to persist between calls.

factStatement: A parameter or local with the same name as an outer variable is a different variable; changing it leaves the outer one alone.
familyName: Reasoning about two variables with one name
measurementObjective: Give the value of the outer variable after a function that assigns to a same-named local.
distractorStrategy: The outer variable assumed changed — the whole point. Also an error claimed for reusing the name, and the two values assumed to be combined.

factStatement: A function with no return gives back nothing usable, even if it printed something.
familyName: Choosing between returning and printing
measurementObjective: Decide which of two functions can have its result used in a further calculation, and why.
distractorStrategy: The printing version claimed usable because the value was visible; both claimed equivalent; the returning version claimed to print. Show two functions differing only in return versus print.
notes: Same fact as FN_FAM07, at the level of choosing rather than predicting.

factStatement: A long piece of code can be split into functions that each do one nameable thing.
familyName: Choosing a useful split into functions
measurementObjective: Choose the split whose functions each do one thing and together cover the task.
distractorStrategy: A split that leaves part of the task in no function; one whose functions each need the others half-finished; one that splits on line count rather than on responsibility. All options must be syntactically fine, so the judgement is about structure.
notes: Ties back to PS_FAM06. Different skill, so a separate reassessment group by rule; noted here because the two measure related judgement.

factStatement: A function that returns the wrong thing usually has a misplaced return, a shadowed name, or nothing returned at all.
familyName: Diagnosing why a function gives the wrong result
measurementObjective: Given a function and a wrong result, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A return placed inside a loop so it exits on the first item; a printed value where a return was needed; an outer variable relied on instead of a parameter. Every option must be a real fault pattern, with only one producing the stated symptom.
notes: Return-inside-the-loop is the canonical D5 stem: the function works for single-item input and fails otherwise.

factStatement: A function correct for ordinary arguments can fail or return something wrong for empty, zero or boundary arguments.
familyName: Behaviour of a function on an extreme argument
measurementObjective: Say what a function returns for an empty, zero or boundary argument.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary-argument result; a failure where nothing is returned quietly; a returned value where it genuinely fails. Distinguishing "returns nothing" from "fails" is the measurement.
